After reconsidering the weaknesses:

W1 (Full year vs partial year concern): CHALLENGE_REFUTED. E1 is from the 10-K filed January 2026 covering period ending December 31, 2025, and explicitly states "Our effective tax rate in 2025 increased compared to 2024, mostly due to the effects of OBBBA." This directly addresses the full FY2025 period, not just partial year data.

W2 (Nature of the charge): CHALLENGE_REFUTED. While E1 provides technical details about the composition of the charge (valuation allowance, FDII reduction), both E2 and E3 explicitly characterize the $15.93 billion as a "one-time charge" related to OBBBA/tax law implementation. The filing itself uses this terminology, so the claim's characterization is consistent with how Meta described it. The fact that it includes a valuation allowance doesn't make it less of a "one-time charge related to U.S. tax law changes" - the valuation allowance was triggered by the new tax law (OBBBA).

W3 (Degree of causation): CHALLENGE_REFUTED. Both E1 and E4 use the word "mostly" to attribute the effective tax rate increase to OBBBA. The claim states the increase was "mainly" due to the one-time charge. "Mainly" and "mostly" are synonymous, so the claim's characterization aligns with the filing's explicit attribution. The filing directly states the causal relationship.

All three weaknesses are refuted by the evidence. The verdict remains SUPPORTED because the evidence explicitly confirms both that the effective tax rate increased in 2025 and that this increase was mainly/mostly due to the OBBBA-related one-time charge.
